newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries seen in doldrums despite Fed on hold.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries seen in doldrums despite Fed on hold.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market just can't seem to win. Despite a plethora of good news in recent weeks, yields are only a touch below levels seen after the Fed raised rates in late March.

Most everything in recent weeks has gone the market's way, yet players expect Treasuries to continue to wallow for the near future, unless fears of another interest rate hike by the Fed are fully taken out of the picture.

"There is still a lot of nervousness and negative sentiment," said Michelle Colley Laughlin, chief Treasury market strategist at Prudential Securities Inc. "The feeling is that all the good news is already in the market.

In April and May, economic growth started to show signs of slowing, a balanced budget deal was clinched between Republicans and Democrats, inflation remained at historically low levels and the Federal Reserve on Tuesday passed up a chance to hike short-term rates -- all of which should be bullish for the market.
The market rallied somewhat Tuesday after the Fed held rates steady and the yield curve steepened, but Treasury prices fell right back down on Wednesday morning.

"You got the budget deal, no Fed and the best economic statistics you could have hoped for the past three weeks. So, how much better can it get? Going forward, there is much more room for disappointment than pleasant surprises," said Laughlin.

Indeed, the first set of economic figures after the Fed meeting was bearish for the market. Commerce Department figures showed a dramatic 19.3 percent narrowing of the U.S. trade deficit in March to $8.51 billion.

Analysts said a hefty 4.1-percent rise in exports, along with a 1.2-percent rise in imports, could push first-quarter growth up to a 6.0-6.5 percent rate, from 5.6 percent seen in the preliminary report.
The data knocked the two-year note down 3/32, with its yield edging up to 6.25 percent. The 30-year bond's price was down nearly a full point, and its yield up to 6.98 percent.

Market participants would not rule out a rally in the two-year note -- which could trim yields from the current 6.23 percent level to 6.10-6.15 percent, or 60 to 65 basis points over the federal funds rate. But they noted there are too many negative market forces at work to sustain a rally.

If the market continued to believe the Fed had only pushed back its next tightening to early July, players said, then the two-year note would be unlikely to stay less than 75 basis points above fed funds, a level which is considered neutral.
"But I don't think the Fed's in a neutral stance," Laughlin said. "They likely maintained their bias to tighthening" at Tuesday's meeting.
In that case, two-year notes could rise back again to their mid-April level of above 6.50 percent, some speculated.

While most of the recent data -- from the employment cost index to retail sales to producer prices -- were friendly to the market, unit labor costs continued to post gains and the "core" consumer price index was up a higher than expected 0.3 percent in April.
Most agreed that the economy was cooling off, but the fear was that it might not slow enough to keep the Fed from raising rates another time or two.
John Spinello, fixed income strategist at Merrill Lynch & Co, said the market had viewed fundamentals as bullish and technical factors as bearish.
"The market is looking at economic factors as abberational," he said, noting the floods in the Midwest and strikes at various automakers' plants likely curtailed growth and skewed the data.
Spinello said that in recent weeks, as the market began to slash odds of a rate hike in May, money managers started to buy.
"A lot of the purchases that needed to be made, were made prior to the Fed not raising the funds rate," he said.
With possibility of a Fed move in July, upcoming economic reports will take center stage.
Players said they are already looking ahead to the May employment report on June 6. Forecasts of a payroll rise around 300,000 are making an already nervous market more jittery.
Meanwhile, the dollar's performance became an important factor in recent weeks, given that the currency has fallen from a high of 127 yen earlier in the month to around 114.
At the same time, New York Fed custody holdings data show foreign central banks liquidated $12 billion of Treasuries the past few weeks.

As for the budget deal, players said that while on the surface it looks to be a plus for bonds, it won't have much impact since most of the spending and tax cuts are backloaded to after the year 2000.
"The bond market seems to be giving us a wait-and-see attitude," said Liz Miller, portfoliio manager at Trevor Stewart Burton & Jacobsen Inc.
"It's telling you that it won't get out of the doldrums until it sees evidence of either significant Fed action or a change in economic trends."
